source.text: Καὶ ἐγένετο ὅτε ἐτέλεσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς διατάσσων τοῖς δώδεκα μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ, μετέβη ἐκεῖθεν τοῦ διδάσκειν καὶ κηρύσσειν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν αὐτῶν.

records.literal_gloss: And it happened when finished the Jesus commanding the twelve disciples of him, he moved on from there to teach and to preach in the cities of them.

en.L: And it happened, when Jesus had finished instructing {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} twelve disciples, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went on from there to teach and to preach in their towns.
en.B: When Jesus had finished giving these instructions to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} twelve disciples, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} moved on from there to teach and to proclaim the message in their towns.
en.R: Jesus finished telling {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} twelve followers what to do. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} left that place and went to teach and preach in the towns of that area.

decisions.choice: when Jesus had finished: the formula that closes the second long speech
decisions.reason: Matthew ends each great speech with these words (7:28; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). This one closes the instructions of chapter 10.

decisions.choice: their towns: the towns of the Jewish people of the region
decisions.reason: "Their" has no clear antecedent; it most likely means the people of Galilee, as in 4:23 and 9:35 ("their synagogues"). Matthew does not say here that the twelve set out.

decisions.choice: proclaim the message (B); the towns of that area (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says what was proclaimed; Readable says which towns are meant.

source.text: Ὁ δὲ Ἰωάννης ἀκούσας ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ χριστοῦ πέμψας διὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἢ ἕτερον προσδοκῶμεν;

records.literal_gloss: And John having heard in the prison the works of the Christ, having sent through the disciples of him, \v 3 said to him, You are the coming [one] or another are we to expect?

en.L: Now John, having heard in prison about the works of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, sent [word] through his disciples \v 3 [and] said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the one who is coming, or are we to look for another?"
en.B: Meanwhile John, now in prison, heard about the works of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}. He sent word by his disciples \v 3 and asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the one who is coming, or should we wait for someone else?"
en.R: John the Baptist was in prison. He heard about the things the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} was doing. So he sent some of his followers to Jesus. \v 3 They asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the one God promised to send? Or should we wait for someone else?"

decisions.choice: in prison: John had been arrested by Herod Antipas
decisions.reason: Matthew mentions John's arrest in 4:12 and tells its cause in 14:3-5. The Jewish historian Josephus places the prison at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.

decisions.choice: the works of the Christ: what Jesus had been doing, told in chapters 8-9
alternatives: works John had heard of only by rumor
decisions.reason: Matthew, the narrator, calls them the Messiah's works. John asks whether they mean what he hopes. The same word returns in 11:19 ("her deeds").

decisions.choice: the one who is coming: the one John had announced
decisions.reason: John had said "the one who comes after me" (3:11). The phrase echoes Psalm 118:26 and Malachi 3:1, where the coming one brings God's judgment and salvation.

decisions.choice: through his disciples, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: two of his disciples, the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: The two Greek words differ by a letter or two; many later manuscripts read "two", perhaps under the influence of Luke 7:18-19. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the one God promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable says what "the one who is coming" meant to John and his hearers.

source.text: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Πορευθέντες ἀπαγγείλατε Ἰωάννῃ ἃ ἀκούετε καὶ βλέπετε·

records.literal_gloss: And answering the Jesus said to them, Having gone report to John what you hear and see:

en.L: And Jesus answered and said to them, "Go [and] report to John what you hear and see:
en.B: Jesus answered them, "Go back and tell John what you are hearing and seeing:
en.R: Jesus answered, "Go back and tell John about the things you hear and see.

decisions.choice: what you hear and see: Jesus's words and his deeds
decisions.reason: Matthew has given Jesus's teaching (chapters 5-7) and his works (chapters 8-9). Jesus lets them speak for him instead of answering "yes" directly.

source.text: τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέπουσιν καὶ χωλοὶ περιπατοῦσιν, λεπροὶ καθαρίζονται καὶ κωφοὶ ἀκούουσιν, καὶ νεκροὶ ἐγείρονται καὶ πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται·

records.literal_gloss: Blind receive sight and lame walk, lepers are cleansed and deaf hear, and dead are raised and poor are told good news;

en.L: [the] blind receive sight and [the] lame walk, lepers are cleansed and [the] deaf hear, and [the] dead are raised and [the] poor have good news proclaimed [to them].
en.B: the blind can see and the lame are walking, people with leprosy are made clean and the deaf can hear, the dead are raised to life, and the poor are hearing the good news.
en.R: Blind people can see again. People who could not walk are walking. People with bad skin diseases are healed. Deaf people can hear. Dead people are brought back to life. And poor people are hearing the good news.

decisions.choice: the signs Isaiah promised for the time when God comes to save
alternatives: a simple report with no background
decisions.reason: Isaiah 35:5-6 promises that the blind will see, the deaf hear and the lame leap; 26:19 that the dead will live; and 61:1 that good news will be brought to the poor. Jesus answers John with Scripture.

decisions.choice: each of these has happened in chapters 8-9
alternatives: only a promise for the future
decisions.reason: Lepers (8:2-3), the lame (9:2-7), the dead (9:18-25), the blind (9:27-30) and one who could not speak (9:32-33).

decisions.choice: deaf: those who cannot hear
decisions.reason: The word can mean either (in 9:32 it means unable to speak). Here it is paired with "hear", as in Isaiah 35:5.

decisions.choice: have good news proclaimed (L); are hearing the good news (B, R)
alternatives: have the gospel preached to them
decisions.reason: The verb is the one Isaiah 61:1 uses in the Greek version. "Good news" keeps that echo and suits every level.

source.text: καὶ μακάριός ἐστιν ὃς ἐὰν μὴ σκανδαλισθῇ ἐν ἐμοί.

records.literal_gloss: And blessed is whoever not is caused to stumble in me.

en.L: And blessed is whoever does not stumble over {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.B: And blessed is the one who does not take offense at {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.R: Blessed is anyone who is not upset by what I do and does not turn away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: stumble over me: be offended by Jesus and so fall away
alternatives: be led into sin by me
decisions.reason: The verb pictures tripping over an obstacle. Jesus was not the kind of Messiah many expected; John himself had spoken of fire and judgment (3:10-12).

decisions.choice: blessed: favored by God, as in 5:3-11
decisions.reason: The same word begins each saying in 5:3-11.

decisions.choice: is not upset by what I do and does not turn away from me
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the picture of stumbling.

source.text: Τούτων δὲ πορευομένων ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς λέγειν τοῖς ὄχλοις περὶ Ἰωάννου· Τί ἐξήλθατε εἰς τὴν ἔρημον θεάσασθαι;

records.literal_gloss: These and going began the Jesus to say to the crowds about John, What did you go out into the wilderness to look at?

en.L: And as these were going away, Jesus began to say to the crowds about John, "What did you go out into the wilderness to look at?
en.B: While they were on their way, Jesus started speaking to the crowds about John. "When you went out into the wilderness, what did you go to look at?
en.R: While John's followers were going away, Jesus began to talk to the crowds about John. He asked them, "You went out to the desert. What did you expect to see there?

decisions.choice: the wilderness: where John preached and baptized
decisions.reason: Crowds went out to John in the wilderness of Judea, by the Jordan (3:1-6).

decisions.choice: to look at: to gaze, as at a spectacle
decisions.reason: The verb is used of watching something worth seeing. Jesus asks what drew the crowds.

decisions.choice: John's followers; He asked them
decisions.reason: Readable says who was leaving and that Jesus asked a question.

source.text: κάλαμον ὑπὸ ἀνέμου σαλευόμενον;

records.literal_gloss: A reed by wind being shaken?

en.L: A reed shaken by [the] wind?
en.B: A reed blowing back and forth in the wind?
en.R: A weak reed that bends whichever way the wind blows?

decisions.choice: a reed shaken by the wind: a weak person who gives way to every pressure
alternatives: the plain reeds along the Jordan
decisions.reason: Reeds grew along the Jordan, and the question may begin there, but the picture is of someone easily swayed (1 Kings 14:15). John was not that kind of man.

decisions.choice: a weak reed that bends whichever way the wind blows
alternatives: a reed shaken by the wind
decisions.reason: Readable shows what the picture means.

source.text: ἀλλὰ τί ἐξήλθατε ἰδεῖν;

records.literal_gloss: But what did you go out to see?

en.L: But what did you go out to see?
en.B: If not, what did you go out to see?
en.R: Then what did you go out to see?

decisions.choice: but: the answer to the first question is no
decisions.reason: Each question expects "no", and "but" moves on to the next guess.

source.text: ἄνθρωπον ἐν μαλακοῖς ἠμφιεσμένον;

records.literal_gloss: A man in soft [clothes] having been dressed?

en.L: A man dressed in soft [clothes]?
en.B: Someone wearing soft, costly clothing?
en.R: A man wearing fancy, expensive clothes?

decisions.choice: soft clothes: fine, luxurious garments
decisions.reason: Soft cloth was expensive. John wore camel's hair and a leather belt (3:4).

source.text: ἰδοὺ οἱ τὰ μαλακὰ φοροῦντες ἐν τοῖς οἴκοις τῶν βασιλέων εἰσίν.

records.literal_gloss: Behold, those the soft wearing in the houses of the kings are.

en.L: Look, those who wear soft [clothes] are in the houses of kings.
en.B: Those who dress in luxury are found in the palaces of kings.
en.R: No, people who wear clothes like that live in the palaces of kings.

decisions.choice: the houses of kings: royal courts, such as Herod's
decisions.reason: John had denounced Herod Antipas (14:3-4) and was now in his prison, not his court.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered (B); no (R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:20, Literal uses "look". Readable carries its force with "no".

source.text: ἀλλὰ τί ἐξήλθατε;

records.literal_gloss: But why did you go out?

en.L: But why did you go out?
en.B: Why did you go out, then?
en.R: So why did you go out there?

decisions.choice: But why did you go out? To see a prophet? Two questions
alternatives: But what did you go out to see? A prophet?
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the question after "go out", so the word can mean "why". With the other punctuation it means "what", as in 11:7-8. The sense is the same.

source.text: προφήτην ἰδεῖν;

records.literal_gloss: A prophet to see?

en.L: To see a prophet?
en.B: To see a prophet?
en.R: To see a prophet?

decisions.choice: a prophet: the people regarded John as a prophet
decisions.reason: The crowds held John to be a prophet (14:5; 21:26).

source.text: ναί, λέγω ὑμῖν, καὶ περισσότερον προφήτου.

records.literal_gloss: Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet.

en.L: Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
en.B: Yes indeed, I tell you, and he is even more than a prophet.
en.R: Yes, he is a prophet. But I tell you, he is even more than a prophet.

decisions.choice: more than a prophet: John is the messenger the prophets foretold
alternatives: a greater speaker than the prophets
decisions.reason: Other prophets spoke of the coming day; John was himself spoken of, as 11:10 shows.

source.text: οὗτός ἐστιν περὶ οὗ γέγραπται· Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστέλλω τὸν ἄγγελόν μου πρὸ προσώπου σου, ὃς κατασκευάσει τὴν ὁδόν σου ἔμπροσθέν σου.

records.literal_gloss: This is about whom it has been written: Behold, I send the messenger of me before face of you, who will prepare the way of you before you.

en.L: This is [the one] about whom it is written: 'Look, I am sending {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} messenger before {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} face, who will prepare {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} way before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.'
en.B: This is the man of whom Scripture says, 'I am sending {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} messenger ahead of {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}; he will make ready {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} way in front of {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.'
en.R: John is the one the Scriptures were talking about when God said, 'I will send {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} messenger ahead of {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. He will prepare the way for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.'

decisions.choice: Malachi 3:1, joined with Exodus 23:20
decisions.reason: "I am sending my messenger before your face" matches the Greek of Exodus 23:20, where God sends his angel ahead of Israel. "He will prepare the way" is from Malachi 3:1, where the messenger goes before God himself.

decisions.choice: your: the one for whom the way is prepared is Jesus
decisions.reason: In Malachi the messenger prepares the way "before me", that is, before God. Here God speaks to another, the one who comes, and the coming of God is the coming of Jesus.

decisions.choice: messenger: one sent with a message
decisions.reason: The word can mean either. Here it is John, a human messenger.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:20, Literal uses "look" and Balanced and Readable carry the word's force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: when God said
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker, since "my" and "I" in the quotation are God.

source.text: ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ ἐγήγερται ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν μείζων Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ· ὁ δὲ μικρότερος ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν μείζων αὐτοῦ ἐστιν.

records.literal_gloss: Truly I say to you, not has arisen among born of women greater than John the Baptist; the but lesser in the kingdom of the heavens greater than him is.

en.L: Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not arisen [anyone] greater than John the Baptist; yet the least in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he.
en.B: Truly I tell you, of all who have ever been born of women, no one has appeared who is greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the smallest in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he is.
en.R: I tell you the truth, no one who has ever lived is greater than John the Baptist. But even the least important person in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John.

decisions.choice: born of women: human beings
decisions.reason: The phrase means all people (Job 14:1).

decisions.choice: the least: the comparative form used as "least"
alternatives: the one who is less (or younger), meaning Jesus
decisions.reason: Greek of this period often uses the comparative for the superlative. Some early readers took "the lesser one" to be Jesus, younger than John, but the contrast is between John and anyone in the kingdom.

decisions.choice: greater: by belonging to the kingdom, not by personal worth
alternatives: John is excluded from the kingdom
decisions.reason: John announced the kingdom and stands at the turn of the ages (11:13). Those who share in it as it comes have a greater privilege than even the greatest prophet.

decisions.choice: I tell you the truth (R); Truly I tell you (L, B)
decisions.reason: As in 5:18, Readable puts Jesus's solemn opening in everyday words.

source.text: ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἡμερῶν Ἰωάννου τοῦ βαπτιστοῦ ἕως ἄρτι ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται, καὶ βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν.

records.literal_gloss: From and the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of the heavens suffers violence, and violent [ones] seize it.

en.L: And from the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of the heavens suffers violence, and violent [people] seize it.
en.B: From the time of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been suffering violence, and violent people are snatching at it.
en.R: From the time John the Baptist began preaching until now, the kingdom of heaven has been attacked. Violent people are trying to take it by force.

decisions.choice: the kingdom suffers violence, and violent people try to seize it
alternatives: the kingdom is forcefully advancing, and forceful people lay hold of it
the kingdom is entered by force, as Luke 16:16 says everyone forces their way in
decisions.reason: The verb can be passive ("suffers violence") or middle ("advances with force"), and the second clause can be hostile or eager. This verse is among the hardest in Matthew. The noun "violent people" and the verb "seize" are usually negative, and John is in prison, so the hostile reading is taken here.

decisions.choice: from the days of John until now: since John began to preach
decisions.reason: John's ministry marks the start of the new time (11:13). His arrest (4:12; 14:3-10) and the rising opposition to Jesus (9:34; 10:16-25) show the kingdom under attack.

decisions.choice: has been suffering violence (B); has been attacked (R)
decisions.reason: The present tense describes something going on from John's days until now.

decisions.choice: the time John the Baptist began preaching
alternatives: the days of John the Baptist
decisions.reason: Readable says which days are meant.

source.text: πάντες γὰρ οἱ προφῆται καὶ ὁ νόμος ἕως Ἰωάννου ἐπροφήτευσαν·

records.literal_gloss: All for the prophets and the law until John prophesied;

en.L: For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.
en.B: For all the prophets and the law spoke of what was coming, until John.
en.R: All the prophets and the law of Moses told about what was going to happen, until John came.

decisions.choice: prophesied: pointed ahead to the coming kingdom
decisions.reason: Until John the Scriptures looked forward; with John the time of fulfillment begins. Jesus does not set the law aside (5:17-18).

decisions.choice: the prophets and the law: an unusual order
alternatives: the usual "the law and the prophets"
decisions.reason: Elsewhere Matthew writes "the law and the prophets" (5:17; 7:12). Putting the prophets first stresses that even the law spoke of what was to come.

decisions.choice: the law of Moses
decisions.reason: Readable says which law is meant.

source.text: καὶ εἰ θέλετε δέξασθαι, αὐτός ἐστιν Ἠλίας ὁ μέλλων ἔρχεσθαι.

records.literal_gloss: And if you are willing to receive [it], he is Elijah the one about to come.

en.L: And if you are willing to accept [it], he is Elijah, who is to come.
en.B: And, if you will receive it, John is Elijah, whose coming was foretold.
en.R: If you are willing to accept this, John is the Elijah that God said would come.

decisions.choice: Elijah who is to come: Malachi 4:5
decisions.reason: God promised to send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5; 3:23 in the Hebrew). Jesus says the same in 17:10-13.

decisions.choice: he is Elijah: John fulfills Elijah's role
decisions.reason: In John 1:21 the Baptist denies that he is Elijah himself. He comes "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17).

decisions.choice: if you are willing to accept it: the claim needs an open heart
decisions.reason: Many expected Elijah himself. Seeing John as the promised Elijah means seeing Jesus as the one who follows.

decisions.choice: John
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name John, since Jesus has just spoken of the law and the prophets.

source.text: ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκουέτω.

records.literal_gloss: The one having ears let him hear.

en.L: The one who has ears, let him hear.
en.B: Whoever has ears must listen.
en.R: If you can hear me, pay attention to this!

decisions.choice: whoever has ears, let him hear: a call to listen closely and take the saying to heart
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the same words after other sayings that need thought (13:9, 43).

decisions.choice: If you can hear me, pay attention to this!
alternatives: The one who has ears, let him hear
decisions.reason: Readable gives the force of the saying in plain words.

source.text: Τίνι δὲ ὁμοιώσω τὴν γενεὰν ταύτην;

records.literal_gloss: To what but will I compare the generation this?

en.L: But to what shall I compare this generation?
en.B: What picture shall I use for the people of this generation?
en.R: How can I describe the people living today?

decisions.choice: this generation: the people of Jesus's day, taken as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the phrase of the people who rejected both John and himself (12:39-45; 23:36).

source.text: ὁμοία ἐστὶν παιδίοις καθημένοις ἐν ταῖς ἀγοραῖς ἃ προσφωνοῦντα τοῖς ἑτέροις λέγουσιν· Ηὐλήσαμεν ὑμῖν καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε· ἐθρηνήσαμεν καὶ οὐκ ἐκόψασθε·

records.literal_gloss: Like it is to children sitting in the marketplaces who calling out to the others \v 17 say, We piped for you and not you danced; we lamented and not you beat [your breasts];

en.L: It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others, \v 17 saying, 'We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not beat [your breasts].'
en.B: They are like children who sit in the town squares and call out to the other children, \v 17 'We played the pipe for you, but you did not dance; we sang a funeral song, but you did not beat your breasts in grief.'
en.R: They are like children sitting in the marketplace. They call out to the other children, \v 17 'We played happy music for you, but you would not dance. We sang sad songs for you, but you would not cry.'

decisions.choice: children's games of wedding and funeral
decisions.reason: Children copied adult life in the public square: the flute and dancing of a wedding, the laments and breast-beating of mourners.

decisions.choice: the children who call out stand for this generation, who wanted John and Jesus to play their tune
alternatives: the calling children are John and Jesus, and this generation would not respond
decisions.reason: "This generation" is like the children who call out. 11:18-19 then shows them finding fault with both John's fasting and Jesus's feasting.

decisions.choice: played happy music; sang sad songs
alternatives: played the flute; sang a lament
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of music each was.

source.text: ἦλθεν γὰρ Ἰωάννης μήτε ἐσθίων μήτε πίνων, καὶ λέγουσιν· Δαιμόνιον ἔχει·

records.literal_gloss: Came for John neither eating nor drinking, and they say, A demon he has.

en.L: For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon.'
en.B: For when John came, he did not eat or drink as others do, and people say, 'There is a demon in him.'
en.R: John went without food and did not drink wine. And people say, 'A demon has control of him!'

decisions.choice: neither eating nor drinking: John's strict, simple life
alternatives: he ate and drank nothing at all
decisions.reason: John lived on locusts and wild honey (3:4), fasted (9:14), and drank no wine (Luke 1:15).

decisions.choice: he has a demon: he is mad, controlled by an evil spirit
decisions.reason: The charge was a way of dismissing someone as out of his mind (John 10:20).

decisions.choice: as others do (B); went without food and did not drink wine (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that ordinary meals and wine are meant.

source.text: ἦλθεν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων, καὶ λέγουσιν· Ἰδοὺ ἄνθρωπος φάγος καὶ οἰνοπότης, τελωνῶν φίλος καὶ ἁμαρτωλῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Came the Son of the Man eating and drinking, and they say, Behold, a man glutton and drunkard, of tax collectors friend and of sinners.

en.L: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'Look, a man [who is] a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!'
en.B: The Son of Man came and ate and drank, and they say, 'Look at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! He eats too much and drinks too much, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is a friend of tax collectors and sinners!'
en.R: The Son of Man came, eating and drinking with people. And they say, 'Look at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! He eats too much and drinks too much wine. He is a friend of tax collectors and sinners!'

decisions.choice: a glutton and a drunkard: the charge against a rebellious son
decisions.reason: The same pair of words describes the rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20 (in the Greek version), who was to be put to death.

decisions.choice: friend of tax collectors and sinners: Jesus ate with them
decisions.reason: See 9:10-11. Eating together was a sign of acceptance.

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus speaking of himself
decisions.reason: Jesus's way of speaking of himself (8:20; 9:6).

decisions.choice: look (L); look at him (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:20, Literal uses "look" and Balanced and Readable carry the word's force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: he is (B)
decisions.reason: "A man" is the speakers' scornful way of pointing at Jesus. Balanced says "he". Inside the speakers' words the pronoun still refers to Jesus, so it takes the deity_pronoun setting except at the start of a sentence.

source.text: καὶ ἐδικαιώθη ἡ σοφία ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῆς.

records.literal_gloss: And was justified the wisdom by the works of her.

en.L: And wisdom was vindicated by her deeds."
en.B: Yet the deeds of wisdom show that she is in the right."
en.R: But what wisdom does shows that wisdom is right."

decisions.choice: her deeds, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: her children, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "children", as Luke 7:35 does. The earliest witnesses of Matthew are thought to read "deeds", and copyists probably brought Matthew into line with Luke. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: wisdom: God's wise purpose, seen in the ways of John and of Jesus
decisions.reason: Wisdom is pictured as a woman, as in Proverbs 8-9. Her deeds are the works of the Messiah (11:2), the same word in Greek, which frames this section.

decisions.choice: was vindicated: a past tense stating a general truth
decisions.reason: The past tense here states what always proves to be so; Balanced and Readable use the present.

decisions.choice: vindicated (L); show that she is in the right (B); shows that wisdom is right (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means shown to be in the right. "Justified" would suggest being forgiven.
